# Running This as a Workshop {#sec-workshop}

The book follows a six-hour, hands-on workshop, and can be taught that way: 300 minutes of teaching in four
sessions, of 65, 65, 85 and 85 minutes, with two 15-minute breaks and a 30-minute meal. The workshop's slides,
at <https://project-delphi.github.io/quarto-workshop/>, are the course resource on the day; this book is the
reading behind them. Participants do the setup in Chapter 3, and the reading on assistants, costs, AI policy
and Markdown, at home before the day.

Exercise times are planning estimates that never fill a block: the rest is for concept slides, showing results
and recovering from a failed command. If the venue fixes the meal time, move the start, not the meal: the meal
belongs between the two parts, so that everyone starts Part III together.

## Before the day {.unnumbered}

- **Collect test-run confirmations.** Ask every participant to confirm the setup check and the test run
  (@sec-step-test), and contact anyone who has not.
- **Windows.** Ask for `wsl -l -v` output showing VERSION 2 before the day. Participants without an
  administrator account, or with virtualisation off in the BIOS, cannot install WSL: pair them with a neighbour.
  The Windows procedure has been checked against Microsoft's documentation and on a Mac; run it once on a clean
  Windows machine before teaching.
- **The network.** Check that the venue's Wi-Fi allows GitHub, uv's package downloads and GitHub Pages, and copes
  with everyone downloading at once.

## The two-minute rule {.unnumbered}

The rule that keeps the room together: anyone stuck for two minutes on a command, an assistant error or a typo
does not debug in front of the room. They paste the exercise's catch-up line (@fig-catch-up), and everyone is
hands-on together again at the next block. Demonstrate the catch-up once, live, early in the first block, so
that nobody treats it as failing. In the 0:15 block, a helper sits with anyone whose setup check or test run
failed while the presenter carries on.

From the Cluster block on, keep the room on the normal route, which copies each block's finished
`analysis.py`. The challenge route, writing the analysis, is for people well ahead of the room; agenda times
assume the normal route.

## Publishing {.unnumbered}

The first publish of each site takes about two minutes from creating the `gh-pages` branch to pushing the site,
and GitHub Pages then builds it in 20 to 35 seconds (dry run, 2026-11-01). Use the wait: show one of the
finished example sites, or explain how the `gh-pages` branch works. The three commonest problems are the first
publish (it must be interactive), a push failing with `HTTP 400` (raise `http.postBuffer`), and a render
colliding with a running preview (stop the preview first); @sec-troubleshooting has the fixes.

## Checking the examples before teaching {.unnumbered}

After any change to dependencies, check that both finished projects still render:

```bash
cd examples/london
uv run quarto render
test -f _site/index.html && test -f _site/london-whitepaper.pdf && echo "Part II OK"

cd ../water
uv run python scripts/analysis.py
uv run quarto render
test -f _site/index.html && test -f _site/dashboard.html && test -f _site/whitepaper.pdf && echo "Part III OK"
```
